title: Can Math Prove Corruption? Turning Tariff Favoritism Into a Bayesian Number
description:
Two senators say tariff breaks are going to the politically connected. Everyone can see the pattern. The harder question: can you turn that suspicion into a number a hearing room has to take seriously?

Short answer: you can't prove intent. But you can measure how much better connected companies do, holding merit constant. That measurement has a name — Bayesian inference — and this film builds it, piece by piece, and then says plainly what it cannot say.

WHAT'S IN IT
• The correction the whole film turns on: not "can math prove corruption?" but "can math measure favoritism?"
• The February 2026 Wyden–Van Hollen letter on an opaque exemption process — and the catch it names: no formal public process was ever opened, so you work backward from the outputs.
• Measuring "connected" in three channels: campaign contributions (normalized by firm size), lobbying disclosures (down to the named issue and the revolving-door hires), and public gifts — the Rolex desk clock and the engraved gold bar of November 4, 2025, and Apple's gold-based plaque.
• The equation: a binary outcome, a logit link, two teams of variables (economic merit as the control, political connection as the allegation), and one coefficient — beta-pol — that carries the whole case. Plus the hierarchical layer that asks whether a firm beat its own industry's odds.
• Ten days in November: a 39% tariff, an icy relationship, the gifts, then a framework deal at 15% — and how a changepoint model tests whether the series really broke there.
• Priors from published research (Lopatin et al. 2024 on the first-term exclusion process), the posterior update, and the Bayes Factor as referee.
• The outside check the market provides: an event study where a zero abnormal return is the loudest result.
• What the math cannot say: motive. The model measures advantage, never intent — and the same research that found politics in one tariff program found none in steel and aluminum. A method that can exonerate is a method that can accuse.

HONEST LABEL
The events are real. The method is real. The decisive numbers in this story are a worked scenario from the source essay, shown to demonstrate what the analysis would return if the data cooperate — nobody has run it on the real dockets yet. Skepticism means keeping those three sentences separate.

YOUR TURN — paste this into Claude:
I have a dataset of regulatory decisions: outcomes, applicant characteristics, and political-connection proxies. Walk me through building a hierarchical Bayesian logistic model to test favoritism against merit — (1) which priors and why; (2) how to partition industry effects from firm effects; (3) what result would falsify the favoritism hypothesis.
Run it on any policy domain you care about. The machinery transfers.

SOURCES

Every claim was checked against its source before rendering; the essay's illustrative numbers are labelled as such on screen and aloud.

AI DISCLOSURE
